ranking.title: Rotations and intercrops
ranking.subtitle: Options based on climate and soil. Expand each for benefits, management and sources.
ranking.unavailable: No compatible rotations were found for open-field, rainfed cultivation at this location.

r1.benefit: Rotating maize and common beans diversifies production on the plot.
r1.soil: The study found production advantages that varied with the season.
r1.management: The research compared rotations, intercropping and monocultures in Tanzania.
r1.care: Choose the cover crop and adapt the calendar and nutrition to the plot.
r1.scope: The source supports maize–beans; it does not test this full sequence with a cover crop.

r2.benefit: Beans introduce a legume before the cereal crops.
r2.soil: Maize and sorghum residues can supply organic matter.
r2.management: Retain crop residues and time planting to available rainfall.
r2.care: Maize and sorghum can share pests: alternating them does not guarantee control.
r2.scope: General guidance; the full sequence needs local validation.

r3.benefit: Intercropped beans can produce food while coffee is growing.
r3.soil: Coffee remains the main crop; beans do not replace it.
r3.management: The guide applies to the unproductive establishment stage of full-sun coffee.
r3.care: Manage each crop's nutrition separately to avoid competition.
r3.scope: Check age, shade and soil; the source does not validate every cover crop.

r4.benefit: Including a legume offers an alternative to continuous cereal cropping.
r4.soil: Colombian trials evaluated rotations alongside different tillage systems.
r4.management: The research studied rice–soybean and maize–soybean in the Llanos foothills.
r4.care: Check drainage and soil moisture before switching from rice to beans.
r4.scope: Related evidence: it does not demonstrate the rice–beans–maize sequence.

r5.benefit: An intercropped legume can cover the soil between cassava plants.
r5.soil: A Vietnam trial found less erosion and nutrient loss with cowpea.
r5.management: The study tested simultaneous intercropping, not this rotation with common beans.
r5.care: Check species, slope and planting dates before adopting the practice.
r5.scope: Cowpea is not common bean; the result needs local validation.

r6.benefit: Plantain can provide temporary shade while cacao is being established.
r6.soil: This is an intercropping system; cacao remains in the field.
r6.management: The Santander guide describes cacao management in agroforestry systems.
r6.care: Adjust shade and spacing to avoid competition between plants.
r6.scope: Choose the cover crop and validate the arrangement for the plot's conditions.

r7.benefit: The sequence combines a pasture phase with grain crops.
r7.soil: Retaining residues can help maintain soil cover.
r7.management: Identify the pasture species and how to end that phase.
r7.care: Check for pests shared by grasses and maize.
r7.scope: General guidance; it does not validate this sequence or every pasture species.

r8.benefit: Alternating sorghum and beans changes the crop family.
r8.soil: Sorghum residues can protect the soil and supply organic matter.
r8.management: Select a cover crop suited to rainfall and the plot's growing cycle.
r8.care: The legume's contribution depends on growth and residue management.
r8.scope: General guidance; it does not demonstrate this full sequence.

why.water_high: Good water balance: the crop's demand fits within available rainfall.
why.water_low: Water deficit: the crop needs more water than the rainfall provides.
why.nitrogen: Adds nitrogen and reduces fertilizer needs.
why.cover: Keeps the soil covered and protects its structure.
why.pest: Breaks pest cycles by alternating crop families.
why.erosion: Low erosion risk thanks to ground cover.
